changes.after: In a pattern, a dot usually matches any single character. Fixed matching treats the dot as the actual dot character instead.

before: grepl returns one logical match result per input string. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; without it, dot is a regular-expression wildcard matching a character. Know which interpretation your input needs.

gsub replaces every match and returns strings; sub replaces only the first match in each string. Neither evaluates the replacement as R code. Complex regular expressions and unbounded external input need separate performance and validation limits.

sub receives a pattern, replacement and text. With fixed = TRUE the dot is literal; sub returns only the first replacement in each string, while gsub replaces both matches here. Neither changes text.
```r
text <- "a.b.c"
cat(sub(".", "-", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n", sep = "")
cat(gsub(".", "-", text, fixed = TRUE), "\n", sep = "")
```
It prints:
```text
a-b.c
a-b-c
```
